transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-10-06 09:00 PT
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Jesse Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Alex Romero (CTO, Skyline Ops), Priya Patel (SRE), Jordan Lee (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, might be rough):
Skyline is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted and dedicated inference. Primary goals: p95 latency under 450ms for short chat flows, burst concurrency up to ~1.2k requests/sec for token-lite ops, and steady-state streaming at ~250 tokens/sec per session for long-running assistants. Security and KMS integration are gating criteria. Next steps: pilot, share benchmark templates, and pricing.

Topics detected: p95 targets, concurrency, streaming token/sec, hosted vs dedicated, private/VPC, SOC2/KMS, rollout plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Jesse Carter: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on — can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Alex Romero: yep, loud and clear. thanks for doing this.
[00:06] Jesse Carter: cool. quick intro — im Jesse, AE at Redwood. with me is Maya, our systems engineer.
[00:11] Maya Singh: hey all. i'll be the deep dive person for perf and benchmarks.
[00:15] Alex Romero: great, i'm alex, cto at Skyline. we run the Ops assistant that does triage for infra alerts and also customer-facing chat.
[00:23] Jordan Lee: jordan here, product — i'm mostly concerned about latency and user experience for streaming replies.
[00:28] Priya Patel: priya, sres — security and compliance are my lane, plus reliability.

[00:35] Jesse Carter: perfect. high level — you mentioned in the form that you're targeting a p95 under 500ms for short prompts and want to support streaming when the model returns long responses. is that still accurate?
[00:44] Alex Romero: yeah that's the baseline. to be more specific, for the in-app triage flow we need p95 under 450ms for prompt sizes under 32 tokens and responses under 128 tokens. for the chat assistant streaming scenario we want consistent throughput of about 200-300 tokens/sec per active session and ability to handle spikes to ~1.2k concurrent sessions for a few minutes.

[01:10] Maya Singh: okay that helps. couple clarifying q's — what's your current setup? are you on a cloud API, self-hosted model, or a mix? and do you have KV cache or prefix caching today?
[01:21] Alex Romero: we do a mixed approach. currently we use a managed provider for most workloads but for sensitive customers we run an on-prem inference cluster. We don't have an efficient KV caching layer yet — that's on the roadmap.

[01:33] Jesse Carter: makes sense. one common pattern is to use our hosted API for most traffic and reserve Dedicated pools for high-throughput or sensitive customers. that gives you predictable capacity and data isolation.
[01:43] Priya Patel: question — our security team needs SOC2 and ability to use our HSM/KMS for keys. can Redwood integrate with our KMS? and what about audit logs retention?
[01:54] Maya Singh: yes — we support customer-managed KMS in Private and Dedicated, and we have audit logs that can be exported. i'll follow up with the specific rotation and envelope encryption docs.

[02:03] Jordan Lee: on the latency front, do you have numbers for hosted vs dedicated for small prompts? we saw in some vendor docs that hosted often adds 50-100ms network overhead.
[02:14] Maya Singh: good point. typical network overhead is var, but our hosted edge regions are optimized; for small prompts we often see p95s in the 180-350ms range for the open models we recommend, depending on model size and sequence lengths. Dedicated gives more predictable p95 — especially if you reserve capacity and pin model variants; you can tune batching/kv cache to push p95 closer to the 120-200ms window for short flows.

[02:40] Alex Romero: and streaming? we need the first token in <250ms ideally, then steady tokens/sec after that.
[02:47] Maya Singh: streaming first-token latency depends on model and payload; with our continuous batching turned down for streaming sessions we can often hit under 200-250ms for the first token on Dedicated in-region. Hosted can do that too, but if you have bursty, high concurrency, Dedicated lets you avoid noisy neighbor spikes.

[03:05] Priya Patel: when you say "continuous batching" — is that the same as your queueing/batch windows? how does that affect single-session latency?
[03:12] Maya Singh: yeah it's our batching window. we can configure it per-route or per-model. for low-latency routes we set smaller batch windows or even disable batch aggregation. that increases per-token cost but lowers latency. for streaming you often trade lower batch sizes for predictable per-token latency.

[03:28] Alex Romero: cost is a factor. can you give a sense of unit cost delta between hosted and Dedicated when we tune for low batch sizes?
[03:35] Jesse Carter: generally Dedicated reduces unit cost if you have sustained usage because capacity is reserved, and you can apply our Optimize suggestions like quantization and KV caching to reduce token compute. Hosted is simpler but spike pricing and multi-tenant variability can make it less predictable. we'll include a sample cost calc in the follow-up.

[03:51] Jordan Lee: we also want to run token/sec benchmarks. can you run a benchmark with our prompt set? we can provide a traffic trace.
[03:58] Maya Singh: absolutely — best practice is you send a representative dataset and we run streaming and non-streaming passes across model sizes and quant settings. we'll capture p95, tail, tokens/sec, and also CPU/GPU utilization.

[04:10] Alex Romero: for bursts — those 1.2k concurrent sessions — is that sessions or requests/sec? to be clear it's concurrent streaming sessions, each averaging ~120 tokens per minute during spikes.
[04:19] Maya Singh: got it, concurrent sessions. that matters for KV memory and context caching. for that scale we usually recommend Dedicated pools with autoscale headroom and a routing policy that spills to hosted or lower-cost variants as a fallback.

[04:34] Jesse Carter: to add — we have automatic fallback policies so if the dedicated pool is saturated we can route to a compatible model in hosted as a graceful degradation.

[04:42] Priya Patel: about private deployments — we need on-prem for regulated customers. what's the lift for private?
[04:48] Maya Singh: Private is heavier lift but possible. We provide a private control plane and an on-prem package. it requires network setup, some infra (GPUs), and KMS connectivity. clients typically pilot in Dedicated first to validate performance, then move to Private for data residency.

[04:59] Alex Romero: curious about kv cache memory — our assistant uses a lot of context reuse, would that reduce compute?

[05:04] Maya Singh: yes — prefix/KV caching reduces compute per request because you avoid re-computing earlier layers. it's especially effective for many similar prompts or repeated user contexts. we'll suggest cache sizes and eviction policies in the benchmark report.

[05:16] Jordan Lee: what's a realistic timeline for a pilot and for hitting production SLA?
[05:20] Jesse Carter: timeline usually — 1 week to get creds and traffic artifacts, 2 weeks for a pilot (benchmarks + adjustments), then we can scope production rollout in 2-6 weeks depending on infra and security reviews. for Dedicated plus onboarding we budget 4-8 weeks to reach production SLOs.

[05:36] Alex Romero: ok that aligns. one more technical — do you support attaching our HSM keys directly, like AWS KMS or on-prem HSM?
[05:43] Maya Singh: yes, we support AWS KMS/Cloud HSM integration for Dedicated and Private. we'll share the KMS integration guide. there are some audit log best practices too.

[05:52] Priya Patel: great. also need to know retention for logs and whether we can push to our SIEM.
[05:58] Jesse Carter: we can pipe audit logs to your SIEM and configure retention. i'll include the export formats in the doc pack.

[06:05] Alex Romero: what about warm vs cold start behavior for streaming long sessions? some vendors drop throughput mid-session.
[06:12] Maya Singh: for long-lived sessions we pin sessions to nodes that keep KV cache warm and avoid cold starts. Dedicated helps here. also model warmup and prefetch of key KV shards prevents mid-session drops. we'll test steady-state 30-minute sessions in the benchmark.

[06:28] Jordan Lee: how should we structure the prompt set for realistic token/sec? single big prompts or streaming chunked prompts?
[06:33] Maya Singh: provide both. chunked streaming prompts are best to test tokens/sec. include extreme cases — long contexts, repeated short prompts, and bursts. also include your failure scenarios — e.g., network blips, partial timeouts so we can evaluate fallback behavior.

[06:48] Alex Romero: let's talk success criteria — p95 under 450ms for short flows, first token for streaming under 250ms, sustained 200-300 tokens/sec per session, and graceful fallback on overload. if you can demonstrate that in pilot we'll be comfortable moving forward.

[07:02] Jesse Carter: that's a clear checklist — we'll aim the benchmark at those.

[07:05] Priya Patel: small ask — can you include a security appendix that describes encryption at rest, network flow, and SOC2 artifacts in the packet you send?
[07:13] Jesse Carter: absolutely.

[07:15] Alex Romero: are there any gotchas from other customers you can share — like common reasons pilots underperform?
[07:21] Maya Singh: sure — most underperformance comes from overly large batch windows for low-latency routes, not using KV caching for repeated context, and routing all traffic through a single region without edge nodes. we document those and include tuning knobs.

[07:36] Jordan Lee: what about model variants—we sometimes want a cheaper 8-bit quant model for low-cost flows and a higher-quality float model for premium customers. can Redwood route by policy?

[07:44] Jesse Carter: yes — smart routing lets you pick model variants by policy (cost, latency, customer tier). during pilot we can emulate both and show economics.

[07:52] Alex Romero: any preliminary notes on concurrency memory pressure? for our model size it's mostly KV and the attention cache that blow up with many sessions.

[07:59] Maya Singh: correct — concurrency pressure is driven by KV/shard memory plus per-session caches. Dedicated lets you size for that and we can set eviction and shard strategies. we'll capture memory metrics in the runs.

[08:12] Jesse Carter: quick recap and concrete next steps — Maya will prepare the benchmark template and run the pilot with Skyline's sample prompts, I'll send Dedicated pricing and pilot T&Cs, Alex will share traffic traces and target sheets, and Priya will share security contacts for KMS and SSO.

[08:28] Alex Romero: sounds good. one last thing — can we get a short deck that maps performance levers (batching, caching, quantization, routing) to expected p95 improvements? that's useful for execs.

[08:37] Maya Singh: yes i'll include that in the packet.

[08:40] Jordan Lee: okay thanks — that's really helpful.
[08:43] Jesse Carter: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the packet and a proposed pilot start date for week of Oct 19.
[08:50] Alex Romero: perfect, talk soon.

[52:00] Meeting end (rough timestamp from recording)

Notes: some technical terms may be auto-transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV cache" as "KV cash", "Dedicated" as "the Dedi pool"). Refer to the attachments for the formal benchmark template and security pack.
